items.title: ncc Webpack build redux
items.body:
This reinstates the ncc webpack build (previously https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/7301, https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/6347), specifically fixing the issue in https://github.com/zeit/next.js/issues/7369.

Careful handling of remapping of externals is provided through the new `exports` object support in ncc, allowing better shared code.

See for example the webpack bundle technique in `bundled-webpack.js` and how that avoids duplication of webpack between usage. The autoDll override approach was also updated similarly to be fully ncc compatible.

Since fully automated multi-entry builds are not possible currently due to the various Webpack issues, these same techniques applied progressively to build all dependencies while retaining shared dependency links will be the best approach for next.js.

items.title: fix(Link): Set focus back to the body element
items.body:
Follow up to #3545. 
Fixes #7681. 

**TL;DR**: `document.activeElement.blur()` reliably moves the keyboard focus back to the `body` element.

## Approach & changes

Turns out [my solution](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/3545) from 2 years ago didn't do anything. The focus moved back to the `body` element automatically if the link element was removed from the DOM, which often happens when navigating to a new page.

However, if the link persisted on the new page, e.g. because it is inside `_app.js`, then the focus stays on the link element. The body element cannot be focused with `.focus()`, because it's simply not a keyboard-focusable element. We could fix that with `tabindex="-1"`, but that would cause other issues. 

`document.activeElement.blur()` unfocuses the current (link) element and the focus then moves back to the default focus element – the `body` element.

items.body:
This allows signifying a page should be pre-rendered during build even though it uses `getInitialProps`.

Adds `prerender` option to `PageConfig` with values of `true`, `inline`, or `legacy`. 

For `true` and `inline` the data will be inlined in the client bundle for the page removing the need to refetch the data on a client transition. In `legacy` the current `next export` behavior is maintained of inlining the initial data and then calling `getInitialProps` on a client transition.

items.title: Modern JS for SSR Bundles
items.body:
Next.js already produces fully independent bundles for the server. This is required by `DefinePlugin` and various other things, and generally avoids bundling server code into the client-side application. This PR exposes Next's internal Boolean `isServer` value, which indicates that a given compilation (or portion thereof) is part of the generation of bundles that will run on the server in a Node.js runtime. The most notable change here is that a new mechanism has been introduced for passing values like `isServer` to Babel presets & plugins. This is done to ensure custom `.babelrc` configurations don't turn off the desired behavior. It remains possible to compile for a specific browserslist/node/esmodules target, however the default is now SSR-aware. The benefit of doing this is that the output better leverages modern JavaScript when the current version of Node supports it, leading to faster runtime performance and smaller output size. Both valuable qualities, particularly in serverless deployment scenarios. Comparing the SSR bundles output of the ["basic" integration test](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/tree/canary/test/integration/basic) shows an expected improvement in bundle sizes when building on Node 10: | File | Before | After | | ---: | :---: | :---: | | `0.*****.js` | 299b | 293b | `36.*****.js` | 985b | 492b | `37.*****.js` | 714b | 296b | `38.*****.js` | 301b | 415b | `39.*****.js` | 413b | 444b | `40.*****.js` | 462b | 386b | `hello-world.*****.js` | 303b | 298b | `hello1.*****.js` | 300b | 294b | `hello2.*****.js` | 300b | 294b **Total:** 4077b to 3212b, a 21% reduction in size. While these bundles are all extremely small, it's important to note that the scaling characteristics are what matter here, not absolute byte size. This percentage improvement is expected to hold relatively true as applications scale. A 20% savings is also directly in line with the runtime performance improvements @mathiasbynens demonstrated previously, where modern JS output resulted in a 17% increase in SSR throughput.
🎉 Updated Benchmarks showing further size improvements | File | Before | After | | ---: | :---: | :---: | | `static/*****/pages/_document.js` | 8627b | 6098b | `static/*****/pages/_app.js` | 6813b | 4637b | `static/*****/pages/dynamic/bundle.js` | 4174b | 2669b | `static/*****/pages/_error.js` | 3772b | 2147b | `static/*****/pages/hmr/error-in-gip.js` | 2981b | 1401b | `36.*****.js` | 985b | 492b | `37.*****.js` | 714b | 444b | `40.*****.js` | 462b | 415b | `39.*****.js` | 413b | 386b | `hello-world.*****.js` | 303b | 298b | `38.*****.js` | 301b | 296b | `hello1.*****.js` | 300b | 294b | `hello2.*****.js` | 300b | 294b | `0.*****.js` | 299b | 293b | `ssr-module-cache.js` | 101b | 101b

items.title: Add next-head-count & remove next-head class
items.body:
Fixes #3494

Removes `class="next-head"` from the children of the `<Head>` component. Instead, a single sentinel meta element named `next-head-count` is appended. The content is the number of contiguous elements immediately preceding the sentinel that _would have had_ the `class="next-head"` attribute.

During an update, instead of searching for `class="next-head"`, the sentinel is located and the N previous elements are considered candidates for `oldTags`. New elements are inserted before the sentinel, and finally the sentinel is updated to reflect the new count.
